title: What Is Thinking?
abstract: Dewey opens 'How We Think' by systematically narrowing the common word 'thinking' to a precise philosophical target: reflective thinking, the only form of mental activity that is genuinely controllable, improvable, and productive of warranted belief. He surveys three inferior forms of mental life — the unregulated stream of consciousness, imaginative fantasy, and passively inherited belief — before isolating what distinguishes reflective thought from all three: the central mechanism of signification, the objective relation between an observed fact and an inferred conclusion grounded in a real connection in the world, not mere association in the mind. The chapter concludes by identifying the two structural phases of all reflective thinking — genuine perplexity and directed inquiry — and delivers its most demanding prescription: tolerance of sustained doubt is not a weakness but the indispensable psychological precondition of honest thinking.
overview:
The chapter begins with a disarming admission: no one can be told how to think any more than they can be told how to breathe. This is not defeatism but a precise philosophical point — thinking is not a technique that can be applied from outside, but a capacity that must be developed from within through genuine engagement with real difficulties. Dewey then conducts a careful survey of four senses in which 'thinking' is commonly used. The first — the uncontrolled stream of consciousness, daydreaming and reverie — is automatic and produces nothing warranted. The second — imaginative fiction and fantasy — may have internal coherence and even prepare the ground for reflective thought, but cannot make claims on belief. The third — passive belief, ideas absorbed from tradition, authority, and social environment — is the most dangerous because it mimics the form of knowledge while lacking its substance. These beliefs 'grow up unconsciously, picked up we know not how,' and their correctness, when it happens, is accidental rather than earned.

Having established what thinking is not, Dewey turns to what it is. His central example is the pedestrian who notices unexpected cold air, infers approaching rain, and looks up to find a dark cloud. This apparently trivial incident contains the complete structure of reflective thinking: an interruption to smooth activity, a suggested hypothesis arising from prior experience, and a deliberate act of looking to verify whether the suggestion holds. The hinge concept is signification: the cloud does not merely remind the pedestrian of rain the way it might remind them of a whale; it signifies rain, because there is a real causal relationship in the world between specific atmospheric conditions and precipitation. This objective connection — the fact that it would exist whether or not the observer made it — is what distinguishes genuine inference from association.

The chapter's third movement introduces the 'forked-road situation' as the universal trigger for thinking: any experience where habitual activity is arrested by genuine uncertainty and where action cannot proceed without resolution. From this emerges Dewey's most demanding claim — that tolerating the discomfort of unresolved doubt, rather than reaching for any available answer, is the cardinal intellectual virtue. Most people, he observes with characteristic directness, find this tolerance genuinely disagreeable and cultivate instead an 'over-positive and dogmatic habit of mind' to escape it. The difference between reflective thought and bad thinking is exactly this: whether the thinker is willing to endure suspense long enough for honest inquiry to do its work.

callouts.line_hint: not a case of spontaneous combustion it does not
callouts.quote: Thinking is not a case of spontaneous combustion; it does not occur just on 'general principles.' There is something that occasions and evokes it.
callouts.insight: This demolishes the romantic myth of insight arriving from nowhere. Dewey is making a claim about the ecology of thought: thinking is always reactive, always triggered by a concrete interruption in the flow of experience. The pedagogical consequence is severe — general exhortations to 'think critically' or 'be curious' are, in Dewey's exact phrase, 'as futile as advice to lift oneself by one's boot-straps.' You cannot command thinking into existence. You can only engineer the conditions — genuine difficulty, unresolved questions, real problems — that make thinking necessary. Every educator, manager, and parent who has issued a vague directive to 'think more' and wondered why nothing changed should read this sentence slowly.

callouts.line_hint: willing to sustain and protract that state of doubt
callouts.quote: To be genuinely thoughtful, we must be willing to sustain and protract that state of doubt which is the stimulus to thorough inquiry, so as not to accept an idea or make positive assertion of a belief until justifying reasons have been found.
callouts.insight: This is the most psychologically demanding claim in the chapter and one of the most demanding in the entire book. Dewey is not describing a pleasant intellectual virtue but a genuinely uncomfortable one. The state of doubt he is prescribing — suspension of judgment in the face of genuine uncertainty — is something most cognitive systems, individual and institutional, are powerfully organized to escape. The pressure to appear decisive, to have an answer, to project certainty is enormous in professional and social life. Dewey is saying that giving in to that pressure is, precisely, bad thinking. The researcher who reaches for any hypothesis rather than sitting with a confusing dataset; the manager who decides quickly to relieve team anxiety; the student who accepts the first interpretation rather than sitting with the difficulty of the text — all are failing at this standard. The consolation: this is a trainable disposition, not a fixed trait.

callouts.line_hint: Ashes not merely suggest a previous fire but they signify
callouts.quote: Ashes not merely suggest a previous fire, but they signify there has been a fire, because ashes are produced by combustion and, if they are genuine ashes, only by combustion.
callouts.insight: This is the chapter's philosophical centerpiece and the most important sentence for understanding what Dewey means by reflective thinking. The distinction between 'suggest' and 'signify' is not rhetorical but logical: suggestion is a psychological relation (A happening to bring B to mind), while signification is an objective relation (A genuinely indicating B because of how the world actually works). The combustion example is precise: the causal relationship between fire and ash exists in physical reality independently of any observer. This matters enormously for epistemology. It means that not all inferences are created equal — only those grounded in real connections are warranted. The person who infers 'someone is having a bad day because Mercury is in retrograde' and the person who infers 'someone is having a bad day because they mentioned a difficult morning meeting' are both doing something that feels like inference, but only one has a real connection to work with. Dewey is drawing a bright line between the two.

callouts.line_hint: forked-road situation a situation that is ambiguous
callouts.quote: Thinking begins in what may fairly enough be called a forked-road situation, a situation that is ambiguous, that presents a dilemma, that proposes alternatives.
callouts.insight: The forked-road image earns its keep across the entire book. It captures three essential features simultaneously: there are multiple genuine options (not a single path); the paths are meaningfully different in their destinations (not merely cosmetically varied); and the choice between them cannot be resolved without deliberate inquiry. The traveler at the fork cannot proceed by intuition alone — they must stop, examine, and reason. Dewey is arguing that every genuine thinking episode has this structure: an interruption, multiple possibilities, and the need to resolve the ambiguity through inquiry rather than guesswork. The practical implication is sharp: if you are never in a forked-road situation, you are never thinking — you are merely executing routines.

callouts.line_hint: general appeals to a child to think irrespective of the existence
callouts.quote: General appeals to a child (or to a grown-up) to think, irrespective of the existence in his own experience of some difficulty that troubles him and disturbs his equilibrium, are as futile as advice to lift himself by his boot-straps.
callouts.insight: This quote has never aged. Replace 'child' with 'employee,' 'student,' 'team member,' or 'citizen' and it applies with full force to every contemporary context in which people are told to be more innovative, more reflective, or more engaged without being provided with genuine problems that make those demands necessary. The boot-straps metaphor is brutal in its precision: you cannot leverage your own position to lift yourself. Thinking requires an external purchase point — a genuine difficulty in experience — that the thinker didn't bring with them. Creating that purchase point is the work of education, leadership, and design.

callouts.definition: A form of mental activity in which a sequence of ideas is held together not by free association but by logical entailment — each step growing out of the last, the whole directed toward resolving a specific perplexity through an honest examination of evidence. Dewey's formal definition: 'Active, persistent, and careful consideration of any belief or supposed form of knowledge in the light of the grounds that support it and the further conclusions to which it tends.'
callouts.why_it_matters: Dewey's definition does two critical things simultaneously: it describes a process (sequential, directed, evidence-seeking) and sets a standard (active, persistent, careful, grounded in evidence). Most of what passes as thinking in everyday intellectual life — reacting to headlines, defending positions, generating explanations — fails one or more of these criteria. The definition is demanding by design: it is meant to identify what thought must be if it is to produce warranted belief, not what thought commonly is. The gap between the common and the ideal is where education must operate.
callouts.modern_echo: Dewey's definition anticipates modern dual-process theory (Kahneman's System 1 and System 2) with notable precision: reflective thinking is the effortful, slow, sequential, and correctable mode. But Dewey adds what dual-process theory often omits: the social and experiential conditions under which that mode is triggered and sustained.
callouts.practical_challenge: The phrase 'active, persistent, and careful' is easy to endorse and hard to enact. In practice, persistence means staying with a difficulty after the first response has been generated — which requires tolerating the discomfort of not yet being done. Most thinking episodes end too soon: the first plausible hypothesis is accepted, the first defensible argument is submitted, the first workable solution is implemented. Dewey's standard requires at least one more pass.

callouts.definition: The objective relationship between an observed fact and an inferred conclusion, where the connection is grounded in how things actually relate in the world — not merely in how they happen to be associated in the observer's mind. Ashes signify fire because combustion produces ash; a cloud may suggest a whale without signifying one because there is no causal link between clouds and whales.
callouts.why_it_matters: Signification is the engine of all legitimate inference. Without this concept, there is no way to distinguish warranted conclusions from elaborate fantasies — both can be internally coherent and emotionally compelling. Every professional discipline that claims evidential grounding — medicine, law, science, engineering — is implicitly built on the distinction between suggestion and signification. Dewey makes the distinction explicit, which is the first step toward being able to apply and test it deliberately.
callouts.modern_echo: Dewey's signification maps directly onto the distinction between correlation and causation that lies at the heart of modern empirical methodology. It also anticipates abductive reasoning — inference to the best explanation — where the quality of an explanation depends on whether the explanatory connection is real or merely associative.
callouts.practical_challenge: The psychological problem is that suggestion feels like signification from the inside. When an experienced clinician diagnoses from pattern recognition, when an experienced manager reads a situation, when an experienced investor senses opportunity — these feel like signification because they are fast, confident, and often correct. But they may be sophisticated association patterns rather than grounded inference. The discipline of asking 'what is the real connection here — what would make this false?' is the practice Dewey is prescribing, and it is uncomfortable precisely because it questions the thinker's own confidence.

callouts.concept_name: Perplexity as the Origin of Thought
callouts.definition: Dewey's claim that reflective thinking always originates in a felt state of confusion, doubt, or obstruction — a disruption in the otherwise smooth flow of experience that demands resolution. This is not perplexity manufactured for pedagogical purposes but genuine, experiential arrest: the thinker cannot proceed until the difficulty is resolved.
callouts.why_it_matters: The implications for how learning environments, workplaces, and intellectual communities should be designed are sweeping. If perplexity is the necessary trigger for thinking, then the quality of problems available in an environment determines the quality of thinking that environment produces. An environment with no genuine difficulties — one where answers are always provided, routines always work, and uncertainty is always resolved by authority — is an environment that systematically prevents thinking from occurring.
callouts.modern_echo: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and Csikszentmihalyi's flow theory both converge on a similar point from different directions: optimal cognitive engagement occurs at the edge of current competence, where challenge is real but not overwhelming. Dewey's perplexity is the intellectual form of this edge condition.
callouts.practical_challenge: There is a persistent confusion between authentic and performed perplexity in educational and professional contexts. A question posed by an instructor who already knows the answer is structurally different from a question the student genuinely cannot resolve — even if the words are identical. Dewey insists on the authentic version, which means educators and leaders must be willing to pose problems they do not already have answers to, or to withhold answers long enough for genuine perplexity to take hold.

callouts.definition: The deliberate, disciplined withholding of belief until adequate grounds have been established — the refusal to collapse uncertainty into a premature conclusion even when the pressure to do so is significant. Dewey identifies this as the cardinal intellectual virtue and the quality 'most resistant to cultivation.'
callouts.why_it_matters: Suspended judgment is the hinge between having a suggested hypothesis and having a warranted belief. Without it, the inquiry process short-circuits: the first plausible suggestion is accepted as a conclusion, and the remainder of the inquiry becomes rationalization rather than investigation. This is not merely an intellectual failing — it has real consequences in every domain where beliefs have stakes: medical diagnosis, legal judgment, scientific inference, policy decisions, interpersonal understanding.
callouts.modern_echo: Decision research identifies premature closure as one of the most costly cognitive biases in high-stakes domains. Diagnostic error in medicine, wrongful conviction in law, and failed strategic decisions in business are all disproportionately driven by insufficient suspension of judgment. The behavioral economics literature (Kahneman, Klein, Gigerenzen) describes the tension between fast, pattern-based closure and slower, deliberate inquiry — Dewey anticipated this tension a century earlier.
callouts.practical_challenge: The social cost of suspended judgment is real and frequently underestimated. In professional contexts, appearing to not yet know is often read as incompetence. The person who says 'I'm not certain yet — I need more information' in a meeting where others are expressing confident views faces social pressure that has nothing to do with epistemics. Cultivating suspended judgment requires not only intellectual discipline but a degree of social confidence that makes it inaccessible to many learners without deliberate development.

callouts.definition: Dewey distinguishes between belief — a commitment to a proposition that carries practical consequences and demands justification — and the passive reception of ideas from tradition, authority, or social convention. True belief requires personal examination; absorbed conviction, however widely held, remains merely inherited opinion regardless of its accuracy.
callouts.why_it_matters: This distinction cuts directly against the common assumption that knowing a fact is the same as having examined it. Dewey insists that the two are categorically different in epistemic status, regardless of whether they happen to agree in content. The person who believes the earth is spherical because they have examined the evidence is in a different epistemic position than the person who believes it because everyone else does — even if they both say exactly the same thing and are both correct.
callouts.modern_echo: The distinction anticipates the difference between deep learning (understanding the reasoning that generates a conclusion) and shallow encoding (memorizing the conclusion without the reasoning). Assessment that tests only conclusions fails to distinguish the two. Dewey's distinction also prefigures Wittgenstein's remarks on hinge propositions and the epistemology of trust.
callouts.practical_challenge: Most of what any person 'knows' is inherited belief rather than examined knowledge. Dewey does not say this is wrong — inherited belief is necessary for functioning in a complex world. The problem arises when inherited belief is treated as if it were examined knowledge: when it becomes the basis for confident action in domains where examination would reveal uncertainty.

callouts.concept_name: The Regulative Function of the Problem
callouts.definition: Dewey's principle that the nature of the initiating perplexity controls the entire subsequent process of inquiry — determining what evidence is relevant, which hypotheses are promising, and what would count as a satisfying resolution. The problem is not a preliminary stage to be passed through; it is the steering mechanism for everything that follows.
callouts.why_it_matters: A poorly formulated problem does not merely delay the solution — it makes the entire inquiry systematically misdirected. The traveler who formulates the problem as 'which road is most scenic?' will examine different evidence and reach different conclusions than the one who formulates it as 'which road leads to the city?' Both problems are valid; they are not the same problem. This principle is foundational to every inquiry-based discipline: the quality of the research question determines the quality of research; the quality of the clinical presentation determines the quality of the diagnosis.
callouts.modern_echo: In design thinking, the reframe is the most valuable intellectual move — recasting the problem in a way that opens solution space that the original formulation closed. This is Dewey's regulative principle in practice: changing the problem definition changes everything downstream.
callouts.practical_challenge: In most professional and institutional settings, the problem definition is treated as given, not as itself a subject of inquiry. Projects are scoped, briefs are written, and questions are assigned before the work begins. Dewey's principle implies that this is often where the most consequential intellectual work should happen — and where it is most systematically skipped.

callouts.misconception: Telling someone to 'think critically' or 'be more reflective' is a productive intervention.
callouts.correction: Dewey is unambiguous: without a genuine difficulty in the person's own experience, exhortations to think are literally meaningless — not merely ineffective but incoherent. Thinking cannot be commanded; it can only be evoked by real problems. The intervention is never 'think harder' — it is always 'here is a real difficulty that you do not yet know how to resolve, and you cannot proceed until you do.' This applies equally to education, management, coaching, and self-improvement.
callouts.still_relevant: Contemporary critical thinking curricula frequently consist of instructions about what good thinking looks like without engineering the conditions that make thinking necessary. This is the exact failure Dewey identifies: transmitting descriptions of good thinking rather than creating the occasions for it.

callouts.misconception: The difference between good thinking and bad thinking is primarily about intelligence or knowledge.
callouts.correction: Dewey locates the critical difference in a disposition: the willingness to 'sustain and protract the state of doubt.' A person can be highly intelligent and knowledgeable and still be a poor thinker if they are unwilling to tolerate the discomfort of unresolved uncertainty. Conversely, a person of modest intelligence who genuinely suspends judgment and follows evidence will regularly outthink someone brighter who reaches for closure too quickly.
callouts.still_relevant: This is probably Dewey's single most counterintuitive claim, and it remains widely violated. High-stakes decisions in medicine, law, finance, and policy are regularly made by intelligent, knowledgeable people who cut the inquiry process short because the pressure to decide exceeds the pressure to be right.

callouts.misconception: If you have prior experience with a problem type, suggestions will automatically arise and guide you well.
callouts.correction: Prior experience supplies the raw material for suggestions, but it does not guarantee their quality. Experience with one situation generates suggestions in analogous situations — but the analogy may be imperfect in ways that make the suggestion misleading. Dewey's point is not that experience is necessary (though it is) but that experience must itself be subjected to examination: is this suggested hypothesis actually warranted by experience, or am I projecting a familiar pattern onto a genuinely different situation?
callouts.still_relevant: Expert error — the phenomenon of domain experts making systematic errors in their own fields — is partly explained by this mechanism. Highly experienced practitioners sometimes over-apply familiar patterns to situations that are relevantly different, precisely because their experience generates suggestions so quickly and compellingly that the pause for scrutiny is skipped.

callouts.misconception: The stream of consciousness and imaginative thought are simply inferior versions of reflective thinking — less disciplined, less good.
callouts.correction: Dewey is more nuanced than the simple hierarchy suggests. Imaginative thought in particular often precedes and prepares the ground for reflective thought — the mind's capacity to generate coherent narrative and explore possibilities is a cognitive resource, not merely a distraction. The error is treating imaginative thought as if it made claims on belief. Reverie is not bad; reverie mistaken for inquiry is.
callouts.still_relevant: This distinction matters for creative work. Brainstorming, free writing, and design ideation all involve forms of imaginative thought that Dewey would not call reflective — but that serve a function in the broader process. The mistake is either dismissing them as 'not real thinking' or treating their outputs as if they were warranted conclusions.

callouts.misconception: Once you have identified a likely explanation, looking for confirming evidence is the natural and appropriate next step.
callouts.correction: Dewey's account of the forked-road situation implies the opposite: the traveler who has formed a hypothesis about which road is correct should look specifically for evidence that would falsify that hypothesis — signs that point the other way, evidence that the favored road leads elsewhere. Seeking only confirming evidence converts inquiry into rationalization. The test of a hypothesis is what would disconfirm it, not what would confirm it.
callouts.still_relevant: This is now formalized as the confirmation bias problem in cognitive psychology, but Dewey identified it structurally a century before Wason's selection task. In practice, almost every professional who conducts an 'investigation' actually conducts a search for confirmation of a predetermined conclusion.

callouts.principle: The nature of the problem controls the entire inquiry — get the problem right before seeking solutions.
callouts.in_practice: Before attempting to resolve any difficulty, invest dedicated time in stating the problem precisely. Ask: What exactly is uncertain here? What would a good resolution actually resolve? What would remain uncertain even after I answer this? The test: if someone else read only your problem statement, would they know what evidence would count as relevant? If not, the problem is not yet precisely enough formulated. In professional contexts, this means resisting the urgency to immediately generate solutions — a discipline that requires both personal self-regulation and explicit organizational norms that protect problem-definition time.

callouts.principle: Productive perplexity differs from sterile confusion — you can engineer the conditions for the former.
callouts.in_practice: Genuine perplexity requires two conditions simultaneously: a real difficulty that the learner cannot resolve by routine means, and sufficient prior relevant experience that suggestions can arise. A person placed in a situation entirely beyond their experience is merely confused, not perplexed in Dewey's sense — they have no ground from which suggestions can emerge. Building genuine perplexity therefore requires sequencing: build relevant experience first, then introduce the difficulty. This is why problem-based learning works best when learners already have relevant domain knowledge, and why pure discovery learning often fails with novices.

callouts.principle: Distinguish between suggestion and conclusion — hold suggestions tentatively until they are tested.
callouts.in_practice: Train yourself to notice the moment a hypothesis becomes a commitment. The pedestrian in Dewey's example generates 'probably rain' as a suggestion, then looks up to check. The failure mode is generating 'probably rain,' feeling satisfied by the explanation, and walking on without looking up — treating the suggestion as if it had already passed the test. In practice: when you find yourself saying 'it's probably because...' or 'I think what's happening is...', that is the moment to pause and ask: what would I see if this were wrong? Then go look for that.

callouts.principle: Build rich experiential backgrounds deliberately — they are the raw material of productive hypothesis generation.
callouts.in_practice: Dewey establishes that suggestions arise only from prior analogous experience. This means that the quality of your future thinking about any domain is largely determined by the breadth and depth of experience you build in that domain now — not the facts you memorize, but the situations you have genuinely encountered, struggled with, and worked through. This argues for seeking out diverse, difficult, genuine problems across domains — not for the immediate value they provide but for the hypothesis-generating capacity they deposit. The person with ten years of genuinely varied professional experience is a better thinker in their domain than one with ten years of repetitive routine, even if the latter has acquired more factual knowledge.

callouts.principle: Tolerate doubt publicly — model suspended judgment for those around you.
callouts.in_practice: One of the most powerful things a teacher, manager, or senior colleague can do is be visibly uncertain in a way that demonstrates productive inquiry rather than incompetence. Say: 'I don't know yet — here's what I'd need to find out and how I'd go about it.' This models the disposition Dewey describes and counters the social pressure to perform certainty. In environments where leaders always appear to already know, the implicit message is that not-knowing is shameful — which produces people who fake certainty rather than do honest inquiry. The practical courage involved in modeling uncertainty is underestimated.

callouts.central_argument: Reflective thinking is not a general capacity that can be strengthened by exhortation or exercise, but a specific, triggered process — initiated by genuine perplexity, proceeding through the disciplined examination of evidence via objectively grounded inference (signification), and requiring sustained tolerance of doubt throughout — that is categorically distinct from all other forms of mental activity and produces the only form of belief that is genuinely warranted.
logical_progression: Dewey surveys four common senses of 'thinking' — stream of consciousness, imaginative fantasy, passively inherited belief, and reflective inquiry — and demonstrates that the first three, however useful or pleasant, cannot produce warranted belief because they lack logical continuity, grounding in reality, or personal examination of evidence.

He identifies signification — the objective relation between an observed fact and an inferred conclusion, grounded in a real causal or structural connection rather than mere psychological association — as the central mechanism that distinguishes genuine reflective inference from all inferior substitutes.

He establishes the two structural phases of reflective thinking (genuine perplexity and directed inquiry), derives from them the regulative function of the problem (the formulated difficulty controls all subsequent inquiry), and concludes that the willingness to sustain doubt rather than seeking premature resolution is the essential and most difficult cognitive discipline the entire process requires.
callouts.bridge_to_next: Chapter 1 has defined what reflective thinking is through its logical structure and mechanisms. Chapter 2 must now address why this specific form of thinking — which is difficult, uncomfortable, and resistant to cultivation — is nevertheless something that education is obligated to develop. The argument for its educational necessity requires examining both what reflective thinking enables (its positive value) and what its absence permits (the natural tendencies toward credulity and poor reasoning that fill the space when reflective thinking is absent).

concepts.name: Reflective Thinking
concepts.definition: A sequential, evidence-directed mental process initiated by genuine perplexity, in which each idea logically determines the next and the whole is directed toward a conclusion that can be justified by grounds external to the chain of ideas itself. Dewey's formal criterion: active, persistent, and careful consideration of any belief in the light of the grounds that support it and the further conclusions to which it tends.

concepts.name: Stream of Consciousness
concepts.definition: The automatic, unregulated flow of mental images, memories, and associations that occupies waking and sleeping life but lacks logical direction, evidential grounding, or orientation toward resolution — and therefore cannot produce warranted belief.

concepts.name: Signification
concepts.definition: The objective relationship between an observed fact and an inferred conclusion, where the connection is grounded in a real causal or structural relation in the world — not in psychological association. Ashes signify fire because combustion is the only process that produces ash; a cloud merely suggests a whale because no real connection links them.

concepts.name: Perplexity
concepts.definition: A state of felt confusion, doubt, or obstruction arising when habitual activity is interrupted by an unexpected situation that cannot be resolved by routine means — the necessary and sufficient initiating condition for reflective thought. Must be genuine (experienced, not performed) and accompanied by sufficient relevant prior experience for suggestions to arise.

concepts.name: Belief
concepts.definition: A mental commitment to a proposition that carries practical consequences, demands justification, and distinguishes itself from idle fancy by its claim to be acted upon. Dewey distinguishes passively inherited belief (absorbed from tradition and authority) from actively earned belief (arrived at through personal inquiry). The two may have identical content but differ fundamentally in epistemic status.

concepts.name: Suspended Judgment
concepts.definition: The disciplined withholding of assent to any conclusion until adequate grounds have been established — the refusal to resolve uncertainty prematurely even when the psychological and social pressure to do so is strong. Dewey identifies this as the cardinal intellectual virtue and the quality most resistant to educational cultivation.

concepts.name: The Forked-Road Situation
concepts.definition: Dewey's metaphor for the universal trigger of reflective thinking: any experience in which smooth habitual activity is arrested by genuine ambiguity, multiple paths present themselves, and a choice among them cannot be made without deliberate inquiry. The metaphor captures both the structural feature (genuine alternatives) and the practical urgency (action cannot proceed without resolution).

concepts.name: The Regulative Function of the Problem
concepts.definition: Dewey's principle that the nature of the formulated difficulty controls the entire subsequent process of inquiry — determining which evidence is relevant, which hypotheses are promising, and what would count as a satisfying resolution. A poorly formulated problem does not merely delay the solution but systematically misdirects the inquiry.

builds_on.reason: Chapter 1 is the foundational opening. It establishes the core vocabulary (reflective thinking, signification, perplexity, suspended judgment) and the core distinctions (warranted vs. unwarranted belief, suggestion vs. signification) that every subsequent chapter presupposes.

anticipates.reason: Chapter 1 defines what reflective thinking is; Chapter 2 must now establish why developing it is an educational obligation — requiring an account of both its positive value and the natural tendencies toward credulity and bad thinking that make deliberate cultivation necessary.
The two-phase structure identified at the end of Chapter 1 (perplexity + directed inquiry) is the seed of the full five-phase analysis of reflective thinking that Chapter 6 will elaborate in detail.
The concept of signification introduced in Chapter 1 is the foundation for Chapter 7's full analysis of induction, deduction, and the logic of evidence.

contrasts_with.reason: Rote drill transmits pre-formed conclusions without engineering the perplexity that Dewey identifies as the necessary trigger for thinking. It produces the passive belief Dewey explicitly identifies as epistemically inferior to examined knowledge, even when the content absorbed is accurate.

Unstructured discovery places learners in situations without sufficient relevant prior experience to generate productive suggestions — producing sterile confusion rather than productive perplexity. Dewey's account requires that genuine perplexity be preceded by relevant experiential preparation.

contrasts_with.concept: Socratic questioning as the primary pedagogical tool
contrasts_with.reason: While Dewey endorses doubt as the trigger for thought, he insists that useful suggestions can only arise from relevant prior experience. Pure questioning without adequate experiential background leaves the learner in empty confusion — perplexed but unable to generate productive hypotheses. The Socratic method is necessary but not sufficient.
